title: Control Block
body:
The general pattern: the kernel cannot store an object's state *in* the object, so for
every thing it manages it keeps a struct on the kernel side holding everything it needs to
know about that thing. That struct is a control block.

| Control block | Manages | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| [[PCB]] (process control block) | a [[Processes\|process]] | state, saved registers, PC, priority, memory map, open files |
| Thread control block | a [[Thread]] | saved registers and stack pointer only; the rest is shared with the process |
| File control block | an open [[File]] | inode reference, current offset, access mode |
| Device control block | a device | driver entry points, buffer, pending requests |

**[[PCB]] owns the process detail;** this note is just the word. If you want what is
actually in a process's control block and why it is a doubly [[Linked List]], read that
note, not this one.

The two things worth noticing about the pattern in general:

- The control block *is* the object as far as the kernel is concerned. A process being on
  the [[Ready Queue]] means its control block is on a linked list, not that anything was
  copied.
- Saving and restoring a control block is what a [[Context Switching|context switch]] does,
  and it is why context switches cost real time.
